gameProject.premise: You are the new student counsellor at Bellwether University, and the four women who teach here keep finding reasons to sit in your office a little too long. Balance your caseload, your studies, and the slow work of being trusted by people who are used to being the ones giving advice.
gameProject.setting: A rain-polished old campus of cloisters, labs and a hilltop library tower, where faculty and students blur together after dark and every corridor has a story.

ai.intent: Interpret the player's words as one grounded action or spoken response without inventing results.
ai.scene: Continue the conversation naturally. Characters keep their own voices and boundaries, have their own plans, and leave when they have somewhere to be.
ai.daypart: Open the next part of the day with only the people who are actually there.

locations.name: My Studio Flat
locations.description: A one-room flat above a laundry, walls covered in borrowed lecture posters and half-eaten takeaway.

locations.name: Bellwether Quad
locations.description: The brick crossroads of campus, always crossed by someone late for something.

locations.name: East Wing Offices
locations.description: A long corridor of faculty doors, noticeboards and overheard arguments.

locations.name: The Greenhouse

locations.name: Perch Café
locations.description: A cramped coffee bar with three tables and a chalkboard of somebody's opinions.

actors.name: Selma Aydın
actors.description: A 29-year-old astrophysics lecturer with dark hair pinned back and a constellation bracelet on her wrist, who teaches deep-space imaging and keeps finding reasons to be in your office after hours.
actors.voice: She talks in careful, measured sentences that occasionally crack open into delight, like: "The nebula in that frame is nine hundred years old — we are looking at a rumour of light."

reactions.skip: She smiles thinly. "No matter. I had marking anyway."
reactions.ok: "That was nice," she says, tucking a strand of hair back.
reactions.good: "I liked that," she says, and doesn't look away this time.
reactions.great: She laughs, bright and startled. "Do that again sometime."

actors.name: Rebecca Osei
actors.description: A tall, deliberate Black woman in her early thirties, sharp blazers over practical heels, who teaches housing law and tidies the chairs after her students leave.
actors.voice: She speaks in complete, weighed sentences with dry humour at the edges, as in: "I'll take that as a question rather than a compliment."

reactions.skip: She doesn't look up. "I had a brief anyway."
reactions.ok: "That was fine." She squares the folder to the desk edge.
reactions.great: "That was worth the hour." She almost smiles.

actors.name: Dilek Şahin
actors.description: A twenty-seven-year-old literature lecturer with cropped dark hair, ink-stained fingers and a coat that never quite dries, who argues about scansion the way other people flirt.
actors.voice: Fast, dry and needling, sincerity smuggled in under a joke: "You're staring at my margin notes again. Say something clever or buy me coffee."

reactions.skip: *snaps her pen shut.* You left me mid-thought. Rude, but noted.
reactions.ok: *half a smile.* Adequate. You're learning my rhythm, slowly.
reactions.good: *taps the margin.* See? You can keep up. I like that.
reactions.great: *laughs, uncaps her pen.* Almost worth the rain. Again, soon.

actors.name: Priya Raman
actors.description: A thirty-one-year-old botany lecturer with a clipped bob, rolled sleeves and permanent soil under her nails, who runs three hydroponics rigs and a research group out of a converted Victorian greenhouse.
actors.voice: Fast, dry and unbothered, sentences that end in a decision; "Right — hold this, don't drop it, and tell me if the pump sounds wrong."

reactions.skip: Fine. I'll redo it Sunday. — she doesn't look up from the tray.
reactions.ok: That's done, then. Good enough for now.
reactions.good: See? You're handy. — a quick sideways grin, already moving on.
reactions.great: Okay, that was genuinely well done. Stay for tea, I've got ten minutes.

stages.name: Dutiful Orbit
stages.voice: She is polished, punctual and pleasant, answering questions about her research with the ease of someone who has given the same answers a hundred times, and she never once says what she actually wants.

stages.name: Wobbling Axis
stages.voice: She starts arriving early and leaving late, contradicting herself mid-sentence, and letting small, unguarded things slip about the life her family mapped out for her before she could read a star chart.

stages.name: Own Trajectory
stages.voice: She speaks plainly about what she is choosing and who she is choosing it with, and she no longer apologises for the space she takes up in your office or anywhere else.

stages.name: Arm's Length
stages.voice: She keeps every conversation pinned to case law and the clock, answering warmth with a measured nod and a question about your caseload.

stages.name: Proving Ground
stages.voice: She tests you with sharp hypotheticals and watches whether you flinch, softening a degree each time you hold your ground without showing off.

stages.name: Unbent
stages.voice: She lets the office door stay closed a minute longer than necessary, says things she has never said aloud, and touches your sleeve without explaining why.

stages.name: Pen and Margin
stages.voice: She keeps every conversation at fencing distance, answering sincerity with a joke and a raised eyebrow, and watches to see whether you flinch.

stages.name: Uncapped
stages.voice: She starts leaving her marked-up drafts on your desk without comment, and gets visibly annoyed if you treat that as nothing.

stages.name: Read Aloud
stages.voice: She reads her own unfinished lines to you in a low voice, stops mid-metre, and doesn't hide her face when you say it's good.

stages.name: Ledger Open
stages.voice: She treats you like a well-meaning intern: brisk, polite, already halfway out the door to the next thing on her list.

stages.name: Shared Rows
stages.voice: She starts saving you a stool in the greenhouse and narrating her rigs to you without checking first whether you care.

stages.name: Root Systems
stages.voice: She lets the work stop mid-sentence, sits down properly, and tells you what the greenhouse is actually for her.

endings.name: Her Own Orbit
endings.text: She declines the post in Ankara, and the phone call to her mother lasts forty minutes and ends with Selma saying her own name like it belongs to her. That night she brings you up to the observatory and shows you the field she has been imaging for six years, then turns the dome light off and kisses you in the dark between the stars. She still teaches here, still wears the bracelet, and now she wears it loose.

endings.name: Two Bodies, One Sky
endings.text: She keeps her office and you keep yours, and every Thursday she appears in your doorway with two coffees and an argument about dark matter. Whatever she decides about the rest of her life, she has decided about this part, and she tells you so with her head on your shoulder while the rain works the cloisters over.

endings.name: The Case We Built
endings.text: Rebecca takes you to the hearing on the Marlow evictions and lets you sit beside her at counsel's table, not behind it. When the ruling comes down she finds your hand under the desk and holds it through the reading, her thumb pressing your knuckles like a signature. Afterwards, on the wet steps, she says your name plainly — no title, no distance — and tells you she stopped keeping people out the day you started noticing her chairs. You walk her home through the cloisters, and she doesn't straighten anything on the way.

endings.name: Off the Record
endings.text: She never announces it. She simply starts leaving the office door ajar for you and no one else, and one evening you find her waiting with two coffees and an unread file she has no intention of opening. You are colleagues in the corridor and something else entirely once the building empties, and Rebecca Osei, who takes everything seriously, takes you the same way.

endings.name: Annotated in Ink
endings.text: She finishes the collection in spring, and the dedication page is one line long and it is your name. She hands you the proof copy in the cloister at dusk, watching your face instead of the page for once. Later she reads the last poem aloud in your office with the door shut, and when you reach for her she doesn't deflect, doesn't joke, just folds the paper against your chest and lets you hold her. She still argues about metre in bed, and still writes in pen, and neither of you would have it any other way.

endings.name: Same Page
endings.text: You never quite put a name to it, but she starts leaving a second chair pulled close to her desk and a spare pen that is always, somehow, yours. She mocks you in public and leans against your shoulder in the dark, and calls that a fair arrangement. Neither of you says the word, and both of you keep showing up.

endings.name: Rootbound
endings.text: Her grant lands, the rigs hold through the winter, and she stops pretending she doesn't check the corridor for you. You end up with a drawer in her greenhouse office and a standing Sunday shift that is mostly her talking with her hands while you hold the tray. She says she loves you the way she says everything — mid-task, certain, no ceremony — and then makes you repeat it back so she can hear it again.

endings.name: The Long Season
endings.text: Nothing dramatic resolves; she is still busy, still direct, still late to her own meetings. But she saves you the stool by the propagation bench, and the two of you keep the trays alive through the term together. It is not a declaration, it is a habit, and she has decided you are part of it.

endings.name: The Long Corridor
endings.text: Term ends the way it started: rain on the cloisters, the library tower lit above a hill that no longer needs you, and your office door standing open for nobody in particular. Four women let you in exactly as far as they could, and you learned not to push, which is its own kind of counselling. You switch off the lamp, file the last intake sheet, and walk home through the wet dark with the strange, quiet sense of having been useful to people you will never quite know.

scriptedScenes.title: Come See This
scriptedScenes.opening: Selma Aydın spots you the moment you arrive and lifts a hand, already clearing a space at her elbow. Whatever she is doing today, she wants you inside it — close enough to see the parts she actually loves. She keeps half an eye on you the whole time, checking you are still there.

choices.label: Ask her to walk me through it.
choices.result: She does, faster than she means to, hands moving ahead of her words — and then slows down, embarrassed and pleased, to make sure you got it. She stands closer while she explains than the explanation needs.

choices.label: Stay quiet and just watch her work.
choices.result: She works, and lets you watch, and the silence turns comfortable instead of careful. Somewhere in it she stops performing for the room and starts doing it for you.

scriptedScenes.title: Two Sets of Hands
scriptedScenes.opening: Selma Aydın turns up with her sleeves already pushed back and something she cannot hold on her own — too many hands needed, or one pair she trusts more than the ones usually offered. She does not dress it up. "You're the one I thought of," she says, and hands you half of it.

choices.label: Take it and do it properly with her.
choices.result: You get it done between you, quick and unglamorous, and she notices how little she had to explain. She stays a minute past finished, wiping her hands and not leaving.

choices.label: Tell her how I'd handle it instead.
choices.result: She listens politely, agrees with most of it, and does it her own way anyway. It ends fine — just fine — and she is already half out the door when it does.

scriptedScenes.title: Both At Once
scriptedScenes.opening: The room is loud and both of them have found you at the same moment. Selma Aydın gets there first, close and easy, and then Rebecca Osei is at your other shoulder with a question that is not really a question. Neither of them is looking at the other, and both of them are waiting.

choices.label: Give Selma Aydın my whole attention.
choices.result: Selma Aydın softens, turns her shoulder to the room and keeps you inside it; Rebecca Osei watches for one flat second, then finds somewhere else to be.

choices.label: Split the time evenly between them.
choices.result: Both of them get a version of you, and both of them watch the other one getting it. The evening stays balanced, and slightly charged, and nobody leaves.

choices.label: Turn to Rebecca Osei and stay there.
choices.result: Rebecca Osei takes the opening and uses it well; Selma Aydın does not argue, just goes quiet in a way you will hear about later.

scriptedScenes.opening: Rebecca Osei catches you between one thing and the next, hand flat against your chest, and leans in with the whole weight of her attention. Selma Aydın is close enough to hear it if either of you said anything out loud. Stepping back would cost you nothing at all — that's the strange part.

choices.label: Close the distance.
choices.result: You let her have it, brief and deliberate, and she makes a small satisfied sound against your mouth. When you look up, Selma Aydın has already turned away — she saw enough.

choices.label: Turn my head, gently.
choices.result: Rebecca Osei reads it instantly and doesn't sulk; she presses her forehead to your shoulder for one second, then steps back grinning. "Fine," she says. "I'm patient."

firsts.title: A Constellation in the Office Light
firsts.opening: Rain ticks against the cloister windows and Selma Aydın is still here, long after the last lecture, her dark hair pinned back and a constellation bracelet catching the desk lamp as she leans over your visitor's chair.

checkpoints.cue: I've spent all week on a nebula that won't resolve — so tell me, is it a crime to want to talk about something that isn't anyone's future but mine?
She turns her wrist so the constellation bracelet catches the light and asks, 'What do you see, then — the plan, or the person who keeps slipping out of it?'

firsts.title: A Long Exposure
firsts.opening: You climb the spiral stairs to the observatory with rain still on your coat, and Selma Aydın is already there, one hand on the telescope and the other turning her constellation bracelet around her wrist. She doesn't ask why you're late; she just tilts her head toward the eyepiece and says, 'Come see what I found.'

checkpoints.cue: She turns from the console, half-smiling in the red light, and says, 'You came—I wasn't sure you would. Come stand where I can see you.'
She catches you looking at the bracelet and turns her wrist toward you, saying, 'Orion's belt, if you're wondering. Most people miss it.'

She steps closer, close enough that the dome's motor hum is the loudest thing between you, and says, 'I spend all day teaching people how to look at things that are far away. Tonight I'd rather look at something close.'

firsts.title: The Long Exposure
firsts.opening: The department has emptied out around you, rain ticking against the cloister windows, and Selma is still here past the hour her appointment ended, turning her wrist so the little silver stars of her bracelet catch the desk lamp. She has been explaining orbital mechanics for forty minutes and neither of you has mentioned the clock.

checkpoints.cue: She turns her wrist again, slower this time, letting the bracelet slide down over her pulse, and says, "You keep watching this instead of the screen. What are you reading?"

She doesn't lean back when you close the space, just goes very still the way she does at the eyepiece, and murmurs, "I'm not good at letting someone else decide things. Go slowly, and I'll tell you if you've got it wrong."

She rests her forehead against yours, breath still uneven, and says, "My whole life, other people picked the telescope and pointed it for me — so ask me, before this goes any further. Ask me what I actually want."

firsts.title: Long Exposure
firsts.opening: The rain has been at the cloister windows for an hour and Selma still hasn't packed up her laptop, though the data she came to talk about has been off the screen for twenty minutes. She turns the monitor dark and lets the room settle into the hum of the radiator instead.

checkpoints.cue: She pulls the constellation bracelet off her wrist and sets it on the desk between you, deliberate as a shutter opening, and says, "You keep letting me stay past closing — I've started to notice the shape of that, and I'd like to know what you want to do about it."
She goes still with her hand on your collar and says, quietly, "Say it plainly — I've had enough people decide my orbit for me, so tell me you want this and I'll believe you."

Her pinned hair has come loose against the desk and she laughs once, breathless and unguarded, and says, "Don't be careful with me — I've been careful my whole life, and I want to find out what's underneath it."

firsts.title: Chairs, Straightened
firsts.opening: Rebecca Osei arrives four minutes early and spends three of them squaring your visitor's chair against the edge of your desk. She sits only once it's aligned, folds her hands, and looks at you as though this meeting were something you asked for.

checkpoints.cue: I've watched three counsellors come through this office and not one of them lasted a semester — so before I waste your afternoon, tell me what you actually do here.
She leaves her hand resting on the chair back and doesn't fill the silence, watching you the way she watches a first-year try to argue a lease clause.

firsts.title: Two Chairs, One Table
firsts.opening: Rain has stopped an hour ago and the cloister stones still shine when Rebecca comes down the law building steps at exactly the time she said she would, coat over her arm, heels ticking a slow, unhurried rhythm. She stops two steps above you, which puts her eyes level with yours, and looks at you like she's checking whether you actually read the case file she emailed.

checkpoints.cue: "You're on time," she says, and it lands somewhere between a compliment and a test, "which tells me you know I'm not going to stand out here in the wet making small talk — so where are you taking me?"

In the doorway she reaches back without looking and squares the two chairs the last students left crooked, and when she catches you watching her do it she goes very still — "Most people laugh," she says. "You didn't."

She turns her cup a quarter-turn on the table, aligning it with the edge, then leaves her hand there, open, and says quietly, "I've spent six years being the one who decides what's enough for other people. Right now I'd rather you decide something."

firsts.title: The Last Chair
firsts.opening: Rebecca finishes straightening the last chair in your office and does not immediately leave, one hand resting flat on its back as the corridor light hums behind her. She looks at you the way she looks at a lease she is about to find a flaw in.

checkpoints.cue: "You've been watching me tidy up for twenty minutes," she says, evenly, "so either say what you're thinking, or I'll assume it and act on it myself."
"I don't do this," she murmurs, close enough now that you can feel the warmth of her, "and if I'm about to, I'd like to know you mean it."

"Well," she says, straightening her blazer with hands that are not quite steady, "that's one chair I won't be tidying. Stay where you are a moment — I want to look at you before I decide what I've just done."

firsts.title: The Chairs She Straightens
firsts.opening: The faculty wing has gone dark except for the seminar room, where Rebecca Osei is squaring the last chairs against the wall, one heel hooked behind the leg of an armchair to nudge it into line. She doesn't look up when you step through the door, and she doesn't tell you to leave.

checkpoints.cue: She sets both hands on the back of the chair in front of her and finally looks at you, unhurried. "You've been standing in my doorway long enough to bill for it — so come in, or go home, but pick one."

She catches your hands and presses them flat under hers against her hips, holding them there, and looks at you with the same level patience she uses on a bad argument. "I want to hear you say it — that I can stop this, at any point, and you'll let me."

Her blazer is over the back of the chair she just straightened, and her voice has gone low and deliberate, close enough that you feel it more than hear it. "You've got my full attention now. Do something with it."

firsts.title: Annotated in Pen
firsts.opening: She comes in trailing rain and drops a battered copy of Larkin on your desk like a gauntlet, cropped hair still dripping onto the collar of that coat that never quite dries. 'Page forty,' she says. 'Tell me I'm wrong about it.'

checkpoints.cue: 'Everyone thinks I'm just being cruel about it,' she says, quieter now, spinning the pen between ink-stained fingers, 'but I've loved this poem since I was nineteen — so go on, honestly, what did it do to you?'
She sets the pen down flat, which for her is practically an oath, and tips her head at you. 'Your turn. No hedging, no counsellor voice — what are you actually thinking right now?'

firsts.title: The Annotated Hour
firsts.opening: She's waiting under the cloister arch with rain in her hair and two paper cups of tea going cold in her hands, and she hands you one like it's evidence. 'You're late,' she says, 'which means you get the inferior cup, and I get to watch you drink it.'

checkpoints.cue: 'Right,' she says, tilting her head toward the dripping quad, 'you've got one hour of my undivided attention before I have to go mark forty essays on the sublime — so what are we doing with it?'

She catches you looking at the pen-marks crowding the margins of the poem she's lent you and smirks, thumb holding the page open: 'Go on then — say something about my handwriting and see what happens.'

She reads a line aloud, low and unhurried, then goes very still and looks at you instead of the page — 'I don't do this,' she says. 'Read to people. I'm telling you that so you know it means something.'

firsts.title: Metre, and What Breaks It
firsts.opening: She has been reading aloud from a rain-warped anthology for twenty minutes, and the weather has not let up, and neither has she — until the line where the caesura falls, and she looks up at you instead of at the page. The pen is still between her fingers, and she has not put it down.

checkpoints.cue: "Here" — she taps the page twice with an ink-stained fingertip — "read the next one out loud to me, and don't you dare flatten the stress."
"You're doing it again," she says, close enough now that you can see the ink smudged into her bottom lip, "reading me instead of the poem."
"So," she says, not moving back, pen still poised as though she might annotate this too, "what did you make of that line?"

firsts.title: Scansion in a Wet Coat
firsts.opening: Rain drums the office window in a rhythm so regular you could scan it, and Dilek is still here at half past nine, coat dripping onto your chair, pretending she came about a student's extension. She reads you a line of Donne, then another, waiting to see whether you catch the beat.

checkpoints.cue: "There — you felt that one, don't lie to me," she says, tapping the page with an ink-stained finger, and looks up with her chin tipped, close enough that you could close the distance if you wanted to.
She pulls back just far enough to see your whole face, coat slipping off one shoulder, and asks, "Say it plainly — do you want this, or do you want the poem?"
"Then stop scanning me and start reading," she breathes against your mouth, fingers knotted in your collar, her whole sharp voice gone rough and unmeasured for the first time all evening.

firsts.title: The Appointment She Booked for Someone Else
firsts.opening: Priya Raman books an hour of your time to discuss a struggling student, and then spends the first twenty minutes talking about a nutrient pump. When the rain starts on the cloister windows she stops mid-sentence, looks at the chair she's in like she's only just noticed it, and says nothing.

checkpoints.cue: I'm not really supposed to be the one in this chair — but the rig's been crashing at three in the morning and I keep going down there in my pyjamas to check on a tank of water, so, you know, go ahead and ask me the obvious question.

I've got two hours before the lamps cycle — my greenhouse is warmer than your office, and I think straighter with soil on my hands, so if you're coming, grab a coat and I'll tell you the rest of it there.

firsts.title: Sawdust and Standing Water
firsts.opening: Priya meets you at the greenhouse door with a rubber-banded bundle of basil and a look that says she has already reorganised her evening around you. Inside, the rigs hum, the gutters glisten, and every leaf is doing something she wants you to see.

checkpoints.cue: "Right — shoes off the gravel, mind the hose, and tell me honestly: does this smell like a lab to you, or like somewhere you'd want to sit down?"
"You've got sawdust in your cuff," she says, thumb hovering just short of it, eyes flicking up to yours instead of the fabric.
"The pumps hold for another twenty minutes," she says, leaning back against the potting bench with her arms folded, chin tipped up. "So. Your move, counsellor."

firsts.title: Cuttings
firsts.opening: The greenhouse has gone dark except for the grow-lights, pink and humming over rows of seedlings, and Priya has stopped pretending to check the pH meter and is just looking at you instead. Somewhere behind her, water ticks through the rig in a slow, patient rhythm.

checkpoints.cue: You've got that look on your face — the one that means you're about to say something that isn't about perlite — so go on, then. What is it?
Come here, before I overthink it. I've been running this particular experiment in my head since the second time you fixed the manifold, and I'd rather find out.
Okay. So that happened. Tell me straight — was that a mistake, or was that step one? Because I can work with either, I just need the protocol.

firsts.title: The Lights Still On in Greenhouse Three
firsts.opening: Greenhouse three glows like a fish tank against the dark quad, and Priya waves you in through the vented door without looking up from the reservoir she's got both arms in. "Nine o'clock's when the pumps cycle," she says. "You came at the good part."

checkpoints.cue: She pulls her hands out dripping, wipes them once down her trousers and nods at the bench beside her. "Come stand where I am — you can see the roots from here, and I want to know if you see what I see."

She goes still with one hand flat on the tank rim and looks at you properly, the way she looks at a failing tray. "You're not just being polite about the rig, are you? Because I'd rather you tell me now than stand there being nice at me."

She turns the grow light down to half, and in the green dark her voice drops with it. "Right — I'm going to stop talking about nutrient ratios. Tell me what you want next, and I'll tell you if I'm saying yes."
